title: Realism in IR
description: Anarchy, self-help, balance of power — Morgenthau, Waltz, Mearsheimer

concepts.title: The Realist Premise: Anarchy and Self-Help
concepts.contentHtml:
Realism is the oldest and most influential tradition in International Relations theory. Its starting point is the absence of world government. Within a state, an authority can enforce contracts and punish wrongdoing; in international politics there is no equivalent. The system is anarchic — not chaotic, but lacking a higher sovereign — and the units in it (states) must therefore rely on self-help.

From that single premise the rest of the realist picture follows. States are the main actors. Their primary interest is survival; everything else (wealth, ideology, prestige) is secondary or instrumental. Because no state can be certain of another's future intentions, even defensive armaments make others nervous — the security dilemma (John Herz, 1950) — and rational fear can produce arms races and wars no one wanted.

Realism is older than its modern formulation: Thucydides's History of the Peloponnesian War (5th c. BCE) and his "Melian Dialogue" — "the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must" — is treated as the canonical proto-realist text. Machiavelli's Prince and Hobbes's Leviathan belong to the same family. Modern academic realism is in essential ways an attempt to systematise the intuitions these older writers expressed.

concepts.title: Classical and Structural Realism: Morgenthau and Waltz
concepts.contentHtml:
Hans Morgenthau's Politics Among Nations (1948) is the founding text of postwar academic realism. Morgenthau's six principles include: politics is governed by objective laws rooted in human nature; interest defined as power is the master concept; political action is judged by its consequences, not its motives; and statesmen must distinguish their own moral aspirations from the universal moral law and from prudential statecraft. This is "classical realism": power politics rooted in a pessimistic view of human nature.

Kenneth Waltz's Theory of International Politics (1979) re-grounded realism on structural rather than human-nature foundations. Waltz argued that the same patterns — balance of power, alliance behaviour, recurrent war — appear regardless of who runs which states. The cause is the structure of the system itself: anarchy, the distribution of capabilities among states, and the absence of functional differentiation between them. This is structural realism or neorealism: states act as they do because of the system they are in, not because of their leaders' personalities or domestic politics.

Within neorealism, a major split has opened. Defensive realists (Waltz himself, Stephen Walt) argue states seek just enough power to be secure and that excessive expansion provokes balancing. Offensive realists (John Mearsheimer, The Tragedy of Great Power Politics, 2001) argue states maximise relative power because security is never truly assured — leading to a tragic prediction that great powers will compete and clash regardless of intentions.

concepts.title: Realism's Predictions and Critics
concepts.contentHtml:
Realism's strongest empirical claim is the balance of power: the tendency of states to align against any rising hegemon to prevent its dominance. The realist canon traces this back to the European multipolar systems of the 17th–19th centuries — the coalitions against Habsburg Spain, against Louis XIV, against Napoleon, against Wilhelmine and then Hitlerian Germany. Cold War bipolarity, on the Waltzian reading, was an unusually stable variant.

Realism's strongest contemporary advocates apply the framework to current great-power competition. Mearsheimer (controversially) has argued that NATO expansion eastward predictably provoked Russia, and that the structural logic of the US–China rivalry will produce sustained, possibly violent, contestation regardless of who is in office in Washington or Beijing. Whether you accept the analysis or reject it, the framework predicts a world that will not become substantially more cooperative until the structure (anarchy plus the distribution of capabilities) changes.

The standard critiques run in two directions. Liberals argue realism understates the role of institutions, interdependence, and democracy in shaping state behaviour (next lesson). Constructivists argue that 'anarchy' is what states make of it — identities, norms, and ideas about appropriate behaviour can transform the same structural pressures into cooperation rather than competition. Both critiques, fairly applied, do not so much refute realism as bound it: the realist framework captures something real about international politics, but not everything that matters.

title: Liberalism in IR
description: Interdependence, institutions, democratic peace — Keohane, Doyle, Ikenberry

concepts.title: The Liberal Premise: Anarchy Need Not Be Tragic
concepts.contentHtml:
Liberalism in International Relations does not deny anarchy. It denies that anarchy must produce the tragic outcomes realists predict. Where realists see structure forcing self-help, liberals see multiple pathways by which states can build durable cooperation: economic interdependence, international institutions, democratic accountability, and shared norms.

The tradition's modern roots are Immanuel Kant's Perpetual Peace (1795), which argued that lasting peace would require three conditions: republican constitutions in each state, a federation of free states, and a cosmopolitan right of universal hospitality. Kant's insight was that domestic political form and international behaviour are linked — a claim that animates much modern liberal IR theory.

The interwar "liberal idealism" of Woodrow Wilson and the League of Nations was discredited by the Second World War, and IR's first wave of academic theorising in the 1940s and 1950s was largely realist in reaction. Liberalism returned in the 1970s as a more sophisticated and chastened body of theory, building on the experience of the postwar institutional order.

concepts.title: Interdependence and Institutions: Keohane and Nye
concepts.contentHtml:
Robert Keohane and Joseph Nye's Power and Interdependence (1977) reset the liberal agenda. They argued that the world had moved beyond a purely state-centric, security-dominated model. Complex interdependence meant: states are not the only significant actors (multinational firms, NGOs, transnational networks matter); there is no clear hierarchy of issues with security at the top; and military force is less useful for many of the issues that actually structure relations among industrialised democracies.

Keohane's After Hegemony (1984) developed the institutional argument. International institutions — GATT, the IMF, the World Bank, NATO, the EU — reduce the transaction costs of cooperation, provide forums for repeated bargaining, generate information that lowers uncertainty, and allow states to make credible commitments. Once built, institutions can persist beyond the hegemon that created them, because they pay benefits to enough members to keep going.

This is "liberal institutionalism" or sometimes "neoliberal institutionalism": not a denial of realism's structural premises but an argument that, even given those premises, institutions transform the calculation in favour of cooperation. The framework explains why postwar trade liberalisation, monetary cooperation, and alliance management have persisted in ways pure realism would not predict.

concepts.title: Democratic Peace and the Liberal World Order
concepts.contentHtml:
The single most empirically supported claim in liberal IR is the democratic peace: liberal democracies almost never go to war with one another. Reformulated by Michael Doyle in two influential 1983 essays drawing on Kant, the claim has been tested repeatedly and is among the most robust findings in the field. The mechanisms remain debated — joint democratic norms of negotiation, transparency that lets leaders make credible commitments, electoral accountability that punishes wars of choice, deep economic interdependence — but the pattern itself is stable.

Note what democratic peace does not say. Democracies are not less likely to go to war in general (they fight non-democracies frequently), and the claim does not imply that democratisation will reliably produce peace in the short run — democratising states may, in fact, be more conflict-prone than stable autocracies (Mansfield and Snyder's classic finding). The claim is specifically about the dyadic peace among consolidated democracies.

G. John Ikenberry's Liberal Leviathan (2011) and later work made the case that the postwar liberal order — multilateral institutions, open trade, alliances of consent rather than coercion, embedded rights and democracy promotion — is a distinctive American achievement that has produced unprecedented peace and prosperity among its members. Critics on the realist side (Mearsheimer's The Great Delusion, 2018) argue the order overreached, expanded democracy promotion in ways that provoked Russia and others, and is now eroding under populist nationalism. Whether the liberal order can survive multipolarity, China's rise, and democratic backsliding within its own member states is one of the central empirical questions of contemporary IR.

title: Constructivism & Critical IR
description: Identity, norms, discourse — Wendt and the constructivist turn

concepts.title: The Constructivist Turn
concepts.contentHtml:
Constructivism emerged in IR in the late 1980s and 1990s as the third major theoretical school alongside realism and liberalism. Its founding claim is that the central features of international politics — anarchy, sovereignty, the "national interest," even what counts as a state — are socially constructed. They exist because actors share understandings about them, and they would change if those understandings changed.

The most quoted line is Alexander Wendt's: "Anarchy is what states make of it." (His 1992 essay of that title is the canonical statement.) Realists treat anarchy as a structural cause that produces self-help; Wendt argued anarchy is a context whose meaning is determined by how states relate to one another. The same structural condition produced the largely cooperative US–Canada relationship and the largely confrontational US–USSR Cold War — the variable is not the structure but the shared identities and expectations.

Constructivism is not, in itself, optimistic or pessimistic about international politics. It can explain stable cooperation (the "Kantian" culture among NATO members) and stable hostility (the Indo-Pakistani rivalry) by the same theoretical move: in each case, the relationship is shaped by mutually held identities and expectations that are not derivable from material structure alone. The framework is descriptive, not prescriptive.

concepts.title: Norms, Identity, and the Logic of Appropriateness
concepts.contentHtml:
Constructivism's most empirically productive concept is the international norm — a shared expectation about appropriate behaviour that, once established, shapes what states do. The classic accounts are Martha Finnemore and Kathryn Sikkink's "norm life cycle" (1998): emergence, cascade, internalisation. A norm is championed by entrepreneurs (states, NGOs, individuals) until it reaches a tipping point of acceptance, after which it spreads rapidly and is eventually taken for granted.

Familiar examples: the nuclear taboo (no use of nuclear weapons in war since 1945, despite US, Soviet, and other capacities to use them); the prohibition of chemical weapons (the Chemical Weapons Convention, 1993); the rapid normative shift on land mines (Ottawa Treaty, 1997, driven largely by NGO advocacy); the emergence of R2P (Responsibility to Protect, endorsed at the UN World Summit, 2005). None of these emerges from realist material logic; each is a constructivist case study.

The companion concept, drawn from sociology, is the logic of appropriateness (March and Olsen, 1989) — actors ask not only "what maximises my interests?" (the realist's logic of consequences) but also "what does someone in my role do in this situation?" A foreign minister who has internalised diplomatic norms may take or refuse actions based on what is appropriate to their role, even when it is not narrowly rational. Recent constructivist work has refined the picture: norms can weaken as well as strengthen, and the past decade has produced a sub-literature on norm contestation and norm decay.

concepts.title: Critical IR: Marxism, Feminism, Postcolonialism
concepts.contentHtml:
Beyond constructivism narrowly defined sits a wider family of critical approaches to IR. Critical theory in this sense — descended from the Frankfurt School via Robert Cox's distinction between "problem-solving" and "critical" theory — argues that mainstream IR takes the existing structure of world politics as given when it should be the object of analysis.

Marxist and world-systems approaches (Immanuel Wallerstein, Robert Cox) read international politics as the political superstructure of a global capitalist economy with core, semi-periphery, and periphery. The action is not state-versus-state but the reproduction and transformation of a world economic structure that produces durable inequality.

Feminist IR (Cynthia Enloe's Bananas, Beaches and Bases, 1990; J. Ann Tickner) asks how the field's central categories — security, the state, the soldier, the diplomat — are gendered, and what becomes visible when you ask "where are the women?" The answers, they argue, fundamentally reshape what counts as international politics: domestic labour as part of the war economy, sexual violence as a weapon, gendered assumptions baked into security policy.

Postcolonial IR (drawing on Said, Spivak, and Bhabha) argues that the supposedly universal categories of mainstream IR — sovereignty, the modern state, the international system itself — were built in and through European imperial expansion, and continue to carry that history. The field is, on this account, in need not just of new theories but of a different historical sensibility about whose experience the discipline takes as default. Together, these critical approaches do not so much refute realism and liberalism as constantly remind them of what they leave out.

title: International Institutions
description: UN, WTO, IMF, regional blocs — design, function, and limits

concepts.title: The Postwar Architecture: UN and Bretton Woods
concepts.contentHtml:
The international institutions of the modern world were largely built in a five-year window after the Second World War. The United Nations Charter was signed in San Francisco on June 26, 1945; the International Monetary Fund and World Bank emerged from the Bretton Woods conference of July 1944; the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) was signed in 1947 and grew into the World Trade Organization in 1995.

The architects — chiefly the United States, with Britain — were trying to fix what they took to be the failures of the interwar period: protectionism, competitive devaluations, the absence of effective collective security after the League of Nations. The UN Charter prohibited aggressive war and authorised collective enforcement; the IMF managed the postwar fixed-exchange-rate system; the World Bank financed reconstruction and later development; GATT/WTO progressively reduced tariffs through eight rounds of negotiation. NATO (1949) and a web of bilateral US alliances added a security layer.

The system has visible structural features. The UN Security Council reflects the 1945 victors with permanent seats and vetoes for the US, USSR/Russia, UK, France, and China. The IMF and World Bank have weighted voting that gives advanced economies disproportionate influence. The WTO operates on consensus, which makes it slow but legitimate. These design choices encode mid-century power; reforming them is one of the longest-running, most consistently frustrated agendas in international politics.

concepts.title: What Institutions Do (and Don't)
concepts.contentHtml:
The liberal-institutionalist account of why institutions matter is the one Robert Keohane formalised in After Hegemony (1984): they reduce transaction costs for cooperation, generate information that lowers uncertainty about others' compliance, and let states make credible commitments that would not be believable bilaterally. The WTO's dispute-settlement system, the IMF's surveillance and lending facilities, and NATO's standing planning machinery all illustrate the model.

Institutions also do things liberal theory under-emphasised. They shape state preferences over time (the constructivist contribution): EU membership, for example, has reshaped national bureaucracies and even how member-state officials conceive of their interests. They create their own bureaucracies that pursue institutional missions sometimes at odds with their members' wishes (the IMF's structural-adjustment programmes were widely resented even when member governments had nominally signed up to them). And they distribute costs and benefits in ways that make winners and losers, which is part of why reform is so politically charged.

What institutions do not do is replace state power. The UN Security Council can authorise force only with all five permanent members in agreement (or abstaining); deadlocks over Syria, Ukraine, and Gaza in the past decade have shown the structural limits. Every major international institution depends on the continuing consent and resourcing of its principal members. Institutions are scaffolding around state power; they are not its substitute.

concepts.title: Regional Institutions and the Crisis of Multilateralism
concepts.contentHtml:
The most ambitious regional institution is the European Union, which has moved from coal-and-steel cooperation in 1951 to a single market, a common currency for 21 of its 27 members, a functioning court (the CJEU), and partial common foreign and defence policy. The EU is widely studied as the most advanced experiment in pooled sovereignty in the modern era — and as a case study of the populist backlash that deep integration can provoke.

Other regional blocs are looser. The African Union (founded 2002, replacing the OAU) has built peacekeeping capacity and an aspirational continental free-trade area; the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) values consensus and non-interference and avoids the supranational moves of the EU; the Organization of American States and Mercosur in the Americas have struggled with hemispheric political divides; the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation and BRICS-related groupings increasingly frame themselves explicitly as alternatives to the Western-led order.

The 2010s and 2020s have produced sustained anxiety about the crisis of multilateralism. The Trump administration's withdrawals (Paris climate, WHO, JCPOA, UN Human Rights Council) reasserted under his second term; the WTO's appellate body has been incapacitated by US blocking of judicial appointments; the UN's failures over Ukraine and Gaza have been visible. Whether the postwar institutional order can survive an era of great-power competition, populist nationalism, and Chinese alternative-institution-building is one of the central empirical questions of contemporary IR. The optimistic view (Ikenberry) is that the institutions are deeper than any single administration; the pessimistic view (Mearsheimer, and not only realists) is that their decay is well advanced.

title: Diplomacy & Statecraft
description: Bargaining, signaling, coercion, alliances — the toolkit of foreign policy

concepts.title: What Diplomacy Is
concepts.contentHtml:
The classical definition, due to Ernest Satow's 1917 Guide to Diplomatic Practice, is that diplomacy is "the application of intelligence and tact to the conduct of official relations between governments." Modern accounts add: diplomacy is about communication, negotiation, and the management of relationships across the full spectrum from cooperation to coercion.

Diplomacy as an organised profession is recent. The first permanent embassies appeared among Italian city-states in the 15th century; the modern embassy system, with its formalised ranks, immunities, and protocols, was codified at the Congress of Vienna (1814–1815) and refined in the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations (1961), which still governs embassy operations worldwide.

The diplomat's job has three main faces. Representation — speaking for the home government, signing documents, attending ceremonies, the aspect outsiders see. Negotiation — bargaining over treaties, trade deals, votes at international organisations. Reporting — transmitting back what the diplomat has learned about the host country. Foreign-ministry traffic between embassies and capitals is the daily fabric of international politics. The leak of US diplomatic cables to WikiLeaks in 2010 produced 250,000 cables that gave the public, for the first time, a continuous-format view of what diplomatic reporting actually looks like.

concepts.title: Bargaining, Signaling, and Coercion
concepts.contentHtml:
Modern academic work on diplomacy is dominated by bargaining theory. Thomas Schelling's The Strategy of Conflict (1960) and Arms and Influence (1966) recast much of foreign policy as bargaining under uncertainty: opponents who cannot directly observe one another's resolve, costs, or alternatives must signal through actions whose informativeness depends on their being costly. Verbal threats are cheap; mobilising a fleet is expensive but more credible.

Several Schellingian concepts have entered the working vocabulary. Brinkmanship: pushing a confrontation toward but not over the edge of disaster, betting that the other side will blink first. Tying hands: deliberately limiting your own options (declared red lines, alliance commitments, public statements) so that backing down becomes too costly. Audience costs: the domestic political price a leader pays for backing down after a public commitment, which is what makes those commitments credible to foreign rivals.

Diplomacy shades into coercion when bargaining is backed by the explicit threat of force, sanctions, or other costs. Compellence (Schelling's term, distinct from deterrence) is trying to make an opponent do something; deterrence is trying to make them not do something. The Cuban missile crisis (1962), the Gulf War coalition's 1990–1991 ultimatum to Iraq, and contemporary US–China standoffs over Taiwan and the South China Sea are all bargaining-theory case studies.

concepts.title: Sanctions, Soft Power, and Modern Statecraft
concepts.contentHtml:
The 21st-century state's foreign-policy toolkit has expanded substantially. Economic sanctions — once an unusual measure — are now routine. The US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) administers an extensive sanctions regime; the EU's autonomous sanctions, plus UN-mandated programmes, have produced a complex web of measures targeting Russia, Iran, North Korea, Venezuela, Syria, Belarus, Myanmar, and others. The Magnitsky-style human-rights sanctions, originating in 2012 US legislation, are now adopted in some form by the EU, UK, Canada, and Australia.

The empirical literature on sanctions is sobering. Most studies (Hufbauer et al., the broader IR literature) find that comprehensive sanctions rarely achieve their stated political goals against authoritarian regimes; they often hurt the population more than the leadership. Targeted sanctions on individuals and entities have a better record but slower effect. Sanctions are now the default response to bad behaviour because they are cheaper than war and more visible than diplomacy — not because they reliably work.

Soft power (Joseph Nye, 1990) is the parallel positive instrument: the ability to attract rather than coerce — through culture, education, technology, ideas, and the example of one's domestic society. The United States' postwar dominance rested as much on Hollywood, the Marshall Plan, the dollar, and US universities as on aircraft carriers; China's Belt and Road Initiative and global media expansion are explicit attempts to build comparable soft power. Modern statecraft is the integrated management of hard, soft, and economic power — what Nye later called smart power — and most major foreign-policy decisions involve all three.

title: International Law & Norms
description: Sovereignty, human rights, R2P, ICC — law's reach and its limits

concepts.title: What International Law Is — and Isn't
concepts.contentHtml:
International law is the body of rules that states accept as binding in their relations with one another and (increasingly) with individuals. Unlike domestic law, it has no centralised legislator, no general police force, and limited mandatory adjudication. It is, in H. L. A. Hart's phrase, a system of primary rules (substantive obligations) without a robust set of secondary rules (about how rules are made, enforced, and changed) — which is why critics have repeatedly questioned whether it is "real" law at all.

The sources of international law, codified in Article 38 of the Statute of the International Court of Justice (1945), are: treaties (binding agreements between states); customary international law (general practice accepted as law); general principles common to legal systems; and, as subsidiary, judicial decisions and the writings of leading scholars. Treaties produce most of the rules anyone actually litigates over; custom does the heavy lifting in areas treaties do not cover.

The principle that does most of the system's work is state sovereignty: states are formally equal, and external authority over their internal affairs is limited unless they consent. The UN Charter (Article 2(7)) explicitly forbids UN intervention in matters "essentially within the domestic jurisdiction" of states. Sovereignty as a doctrine dates to the Peace of Westphalia (1648), though contemporary historians (Stéphane Beaulac and others) argue the "Westphalian myth" oversimplifies what 1648 actually did. The doctrine is strong but not absolute, and most of the recent argument in international law is about its boundaries.

concepts.title: Human Rights and the Postwar Revolution
concepts.contentHtml:
The most consequential post-1945 transformation has been the rise of international human rights law. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948), drafted under Eleanor Roosevelt's chairmanship, declared a non-binding catalogue of rights belonging to every person regardless of citizenship. Two binding 1966 covenants — on civil and political rights, and on economic, social and cultural rights — gave the Declaration legal force.

Regional human-rights systems have built the densest case law. The European Convention on Human Rights (1950), administered by the Strasbourg court, allows individuals to sue states; its judgments bind 46 member states and have reshaped law on press freedom, surveillance, asylum, and discrimination. The Inter-American and African systems have parallel courts and commissions. Their jurisprudence, especially the European Court's, provides the most empirically active body of law on rights.

The most contested human-rights instruments are those that carry criminal liability for individuals. The Genocide Convention (1948), the Geneva Conventions (1949) on the laws of war, and the Rome Statute (1998) creating the International Criminal Court constitute a regime under which heads of state and military commanders can in principle be tried for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and aggression. The ICC at The Hague has issued arrest warrants against Omar al-Bashir, Muammar Gaddafi, Vladimir Putin (2023), and Benjamin Netanyahu (2024); enforcement of those indictments depends on member states' willingness to arrest, which has been highly uneven.

concepts.title: R2P, Use of Force, and Law's Limits
concepts.contentHtml:
One of international law's most ambitious recent moves is the Responsibility to Protect (R2P), endorsed at the 2005 UN World Summit. The doctrine holds that states have a primary responsibility to protect their populations from genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing, and crimes against humanity; if they manifestly fail, the international community — through the Security Council — has a responsibility to act, including with force as a last resort.

R2P's record is uneven. The 2011 Libya intervention (Security Council Resolution 1973) was authorised under R2P logic. The Russian and Chinese view that NATO exceeded its mandate by pursuing regime change in Tripoli is widely cited as having frozen Council action on Syria from 2011 onwards. Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, framed by Moscow as a humanitarian intervention against a fictional "genocide," demonstrated the doctrine's vulnerability to bad-faith invocation.

The deeper structural limits of international law are well-known. Enforcement depends on states with no obligation to enforce; the Security Council's permanent members can veto action against themselves and their allies. Compliance with rulings depends on the political will of the losing party. The ICC, the WTO Appellate Body, and the European Court of Human Rights all face episodes of withdrawal, non-compliance, or paralysis. The optimistic case (Harold Koh's transnational legal process) is that states comply with international law most of the time because internalising it serves their long-run interests; the pessimistic case is that international law works only where states want it to work, and great-power exception remains the rule. Both descriptions capture parts of how the system actually operates.
